stat_summary: Red-green colour vision deficiency, the most common form of colour blindness, occurs in about 1 in 12 men and 1 in 200 women among people of Northern European ancestry, according to NIH MedlinePlus Genetics. The condition is inherited in an X-linked pattern, which is why it is much more frequent in men.
stat_source_title: Color vision deficiency, NIH MedlinePlus Genetics

male.headline: Cook Until Golden Brown: One in 12 Men Are Guessing, and Society Thinks It's Hilarious
male.standfirst: Official medical figures confirm what every bloke already knows from a packet of wires and a jumper that was definitely green in the shop: a very common disadvantage is still treated as a punchline.
male.image_caption: Pete, 42, conducting a 50-50 on the fuse box.
body_paragraphs: Official medical figures have confirmed what every bloke already knows from a packet of wires and a jumper that was definitely green in the shop: red-green colour blindness is not a rare curiosity. Among people of Northern European ancestry it affects about 1 in 12 men – and about 1 in 200 women – and the world of traffic lights, pie charts, tube maps and the instruction to “cook until golden brown” has been designed as if they were all having everyone on.

“I held up two reels of cable and picked the one that looked slightly more like a banana,” said Pete, 42, from Portsmouth. “Everybody thought it was hilarious. Nobody offered to write ‘live’ on anything.”

Researchers note that the condition is X-linked, which is why it lands so much more often on men, and that sharpness of vision is usually fine, which is why it is so easy to treat as a gag. Campaigners are already calling for a National Ishihara Day, and for every public map, traffic-light salad and barbecue instruction to come with, in their words, “a version a bloke can actually use”.
Yet where is the outrage? Where is the documentary? Britain’s unacknowledged one-in-twelve squints on, alone, with only a 50-50 guess for company.
male.pull_quote: Everybody thought it was hilarious. Nobody offered to write ‘live’ on anything.

female.headline: Head of Quality Control: Women Spend Their Lives Answering 'Does This Match?', and It's No Coincidence
female.standfirst: The same figures that show colour blindness is rare in women also explain a familiar unpaid job: when 1 in 12 men cannot tell the difference, someone has to, and it is never put on the mortgage.
female.image_caption: Linda, 46, ruling on two jumpers that are, officially, both brown.
body_paragraphs: The same official figures that show red-green colour blindness is rare in women – about 1 in 200, against 1 in 12 men – also explain a job that never appears on any timesheet. When so many of the men in a woman’s life cannot reliably tell the shades apart, she becomes the household’s unofficial colour department, on call for jumpers, burgers and anything with a wire.

“He held up two socks that were, to him, identical. One was navy. One was the school jumper,” said Linda, 46, from York. “I have been head of quality control since 2009, and nobody has ever put it on the mortgage.”

Because the condition is so much more common in men, the knock-on labour – matching the uniform, reading the chart, confirming that the burger is not, in fact, still raw – falls, day after day, to women. Campaigners are demanding a Colour Consultancy Allowance and a national apology for the phrase “you choose, you’re better at this”.
Until then, the country’s unpaid shade-matchers will keep holding things up to the window, one almost-identical jumper at a time.
female.pull_quote: I have been head of quality control since 2009, and nobody has ever put it on the mortgage.
